Here's the complete parts list for the feeder — everything you need to build the physical dispenser, pulled together from the hardware BOM and the servo work. Grouped so you can shop it in one go.

## 1. Electronics

| Item | Qty | Spec / why |
|---|---|---|
| **MG90S servo** | **2** | **Metal gear**, standard **180°** (not 360°/continuous). Not the SG90 — its plastic gears strip when kibble jams the rotor. Buy 2 so a failure mid-demo doesn't sink you. |
| **5 V power supply, ≥ 2 A** | 1 | For the servo **only**. A stalling MG90S pulls ~1 A in spikes; powering it from the board's 3.3 V/5 V pin browns out the ESP32-S3 and resets it mid-feed. |
| **Electrolytic capacitor, 470–1000 µF / 16 V** | 1 | Across the servo's 5 V and GND, close to the servo — absorbs the start-up inrush. |
| **Female-to-female jumper wires** | ~4 | The servo ends in a 3-pin female header; you need to reach the board's GPIO43 (signal) and tie grounds. |
| **Small breadboard or screw terminal** | 1 | To join the board GND and the 5 V-supply GND (**common ground is mandatory**). |

## 2. Fasteners (for the printed parts)

| Item | Qty | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **M3 screws (~35–40 mm)** | 4 | Bolt the two end plates to the housing posts. |
| **M2 self-tapping screws (~6–8 mm)** | 2 | Mount the servo body to the servo plate. |
| Servo horn (round) + its screw | — | Usually **included** with the MG90S — drives the rotor. |

## 3. 3D printing

| Item | Note |
|---|---|
| **PLA or PETG filament, 1.75 mm** | PLA is fine for dry kibble; PETG if you want washable parts. |
| Access to a 3D printer | The 5 printable parts (rotor, housing, 2 plates, hopper) are in [`hardware/stl/`](hardware/stl/) — all print **without supports**. |

## 4. For calibration & assembly (you may already have these)

- **Calipers** — to verify the MG90S dimensions against the `.scad` *before* printing the servo plate (clone servos vary by a mm or two; it's the one part where that matters).
- **A kitchen scale (0.1 g)** — the one-time calibration: dispense one pocket, weigh it, put the number in `GRAMS_PER_POCKET`.

## What you do **not** need
No motor driver, no level shifter, no external PWM chip — the ESP32-S3 generates the 50 Hz servo signal in hardware (LEDC) and drives the servo's signal pin directly at 3.3 V.

---

**One thing to verify when it arrives:** the servo signal is on **GPIO43**, which is also UART0 TX. Your console is USB-CDC so it *should* be free — but on first power-up with the servo attached, watch for random twitching at boot (that'd be console bytes leaking onto the pin). If it happens, it's a one-line move to GPIO40/41/42/47/48.

The full wiring diagram and assembly order are in [`hardware/README.md`](hardware/README.md). Want me to render that as a clean web page too, like the READMEs?

That email is the authoritative source — thanks for pasting it, it answers this better than the docs would. Here's what it actually says about your question:

## When do you submit?

**The submission window is July 1 – September 20.** You don't wait until "the whole project is done" — submission is a git push to your team repo, and you can **keep pushing updates right up to Sept 20**. So the right move is to submit your working repo *now-ish* (you're safely in for the screening round), then keep improving it until the deadline. Don't hold everything back for a "finished" moment.

The timeline has two stages:
- **First review: Sept 21–30** — repo-based screening (code + logs + README/docs).
- **Finals / Awards: TBA** — this is where a live/physical demo carries weight.

## Is a physical product *required* to submit?

Based on this email: **not as a hard gate, but strongly valued.** Two signals:

1. The process explicitly includes a **"部署验证 / deployment verification"** step — the system must actually *run on the hardware*. VelaPaw already passes this: recognition, feeding logic, scheduling, display, persistence all run on the ESP32-S3 board. That's the core deliverable, and you have it.
2. A fully-assembled physical feeder (servo + rotor + hopper) isn't stated as a mandatory submission requirement, **but** it directly lifts your **Project Completeness (20 pts)** score and is what makes the **finals defense** compelling. So it's "not required to submit, but a real advantage."

Honest caveat: this email is the operational summary. The precise "required deliverables" list lives in the linked **Contest Overview** — worth a look — but nothing here says you must have a finished physical device by Sept 20.

## The JLC 400-yuan subsidy is *for exactly this*

The **嘉立创 (JLCPCB) 400-yuan coupon covers PCB + SMT + 3D printing** — which is precisely your remaining physical work:
- **3D printing** → print your feeder parts (rotor, housing, 2 plates, hopper) at JLC instead of needing your own printer.
- **PCB + SMT** → optionally a small board for the servo signal + external-5 V + ground + capacitor, cleaner than jumper wires for the demo.

The organizers are literally funding the physical build. Claim it (per the email, there's a checklist for benefit-distribution status).

## My recommendation

You're on **July 18**, deadline **Sept 20** — about two months. So:

1. **Submit the working repo soon** (code + logs + docs are all done) so you're locked in for screening. Keep pushing improvements until Sept 20.
2. **Use the JLC coupon** to 3D-print the feeder and (optionally) a small servo PCB, plus buy the MG90S + 5 V supply from the parts list.
3. **Assemble the physical feeder for the finals demo** — that's where it pays off most, and you have time.

So: no, you don't have to wait for the physical build to submit — submit the working system now, and build the physical feeder (subsidized) toward the finals. Want me to sanity-check your repo is submission-ready (what's committed vs still local), so you can push with confidence?
so do i still need fasterners?

Yes — you still need the fasteners. The JLC coupon (PCB + SMT + **3D printing**) gives you the **plastic parts**, but 3D printing doesn't include metal screws. Fasteners are separate, standard hardware you buy on their own — and they're cheap (a small M2/M3 screw assortment is ~¥10–20).

Here's the honest breakdown of what's actually unavoidable:

| Fastener | Needed? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **2 × M2 self-tapping** (servo → plate) | **Yes, unavoidable** | Servos mount via screw holes — there's no clean way around this. |
| Servo horn screw | Comes **with the MG90S** | Don't buy separately. |
| **4 × M3** (end plates → housing) | Yes in the current design — **but optional** | These just hold the drum together; a snap-fit redesign could remove them. |

So at minimum you need the **2× M2 for the servo**. The **4× M3 plate screws** are the only ones I could design out.

If you want to minimize bought hardware, I can rework the `.scad` so the end plates **snap-fit / press-fit** onto the housing instead of bolting — that would drop the M3 screws entirely, leaving only the two M2 servo screws (which you can't avoid). But honestly, a ¥10 screw kit is simpler and more reliable for a demo than fighting print tolerances on snap-fits.

My recommendation: **just buy a cheap M2/M3 screw assortment** — it's trivial cost, and screws hold up better for repeated assembly/disassembly during testing and the defense. Only go screwless if you specifically want to avoid sourcing any metal hardware.

Want me to redesign the plates for snap-fit (screwless except the servo), or leave it screwed and you grab a screw kit?
what about pla/petg

Same logic — if you use the **JLC 3D-printing coupon, you don't buy PLA/PETG at all.** JLC is a *print service*: you upload the STL, they print it with **their** material and ship it to you. The filament (and the printer) were only in my list for the case where you print it yourself. Using the subsidy, cross both off.

What you do instead is **pick the material when you place the order.** And here the choice matters, because JLC's 3D options aren't PLA/PETG by default — they're mostly **resin (SLA)** and **nylon (SLS)**, and that affects durability:

| Part | Load | Best JLC material |
|---|---|---|
| **Rotor + housing** | Moving/wearing — takes real mechanical stress | **Nylon (SLS)** — tough, slightly flexible; ideal. A "tough/ABS-like resin" also works. **Avoid standard resin** — it's brittle and the rotor vanes could crack. |
| **Hopper + end plates** | Low stress | Anything — standard resin is fine here. |

So the honest summary of your "what to buy" list, adjusted for the subsidy:

- ❌ **PLA/PETG filament** — not needed (JLC supplies material)
- ❌ **3D printer** — not needed (JLC prints it)
- ✅ **MG90S servo ×2, 5 V supply, capacitor, jumpers** — still buy
- ✅ **M2 screws** (servo mount) — still buy; M3 optional
- ✅ **Kitchen scale + calipers** — for calibration/verification (you may have these)

One practical note: JLC will likely quote the **rotor and housing in nylon** as the pricier items — that's exactly where the 400-yuan coupon helps. Print the load-bearing parts in nylon and the rest in cheap resin to stretch the coupon.

So: no filament needed if you go through JLC — just choose **nylon for the rotor/housing** at order time. Want me to add a short "ordering from JLC" note (recommended material per part + orientation) to `hardware/README.md` so it's captured for when you place the order?
So what improvements can be made to the system

Good question to step back on. VelaPaw is already feature-rich, so the improvements that matter now aren't more menu items — they're the ones that close a real gap in the *product story* or the *technical depth*. Here's my honest ranking, tied to what actually scores.

## The standout: close the feeding loop with a load cell

Right now feeding is **open-loop** — you command the servo to index N pockets and *assume* N grams came out. You never actually verify food was dispensed, or detect an empty hopper, or know when a pet is eating.

A **load cell + HX711** under the bowl (~¥10, and the JLC coupon can even PCB it) turns this into **closed-loop portion control**: dispense *until the bowl gains N grams*, detect a jam or empty hopper (commanded but no weight change), and sense when a pet is actually eating. This is the single biggest credibility upgrade because it makes your core claim — *per-pet portion control* — **verified rather than assumed**. It hits **Technical Difficulty (30)** and **Product Innovation (20)** at once, and it's a genuine hardware+driver+integration piece (HX711 over GPIO, calibration, feed-loop logic). It's real work, but it's the improvement that most elevates the product.

## Recognition robustness: a "is this even a pet?" gate

The weakest technical link is the false-accept we found (a chair scored "bob 0.71"). Good enrollment mitigates it, but there's no gate that *rejects non-pets*. Adding a lightweight pet-presence check before running identity — or gating recognition on the load cell / an approach sensor detecting an actual animal — would make recognition trustworthy against arbitrary objects. This is an honest weakness a judge could probe in the defense; fixing it is defensible AI engineering.

## Completeness: persist feeding history to flash + real calendar days

You chose to leave this, and that's fine — but it's the honest upgrade to the **health-monitoring** story. Today the trends are RAM-only (wiped on reset) and days advance via a demo button, seeded with synthetic data. Persisting to flash (we have the pattern) + auto-rolling on the RTC's real day would make "here's what your cat ate each of the last 7 days, and it survived a reboot" *true*. Feeds **Project Completeness (20)**.

## Smaller, cheaper polish

- **Approach sensor (PIR/ToF)** to trigger recognition only when a pet nears — saves power, stops continuous camera streaming (also sidesteps the residual camera-DMA concern).
- **Fix the camera geometry** — mount it at cat-head height facing the approach path (we discussed this; it's a print/enclosure decision, not new hardware).
- **A feed chime** (buzzer) — small, but makes the demo feel finished.
- **Retrain identity on individual pets** (not breed-level) for sharper discrimination — needs data + GPU, so it's the highest-effort/lowest-certainty item.

## My recommendation

If you want *one* thing that most strengthens the system for the finals: **the load cell / closed-loop feeding.** It's fundable by the JLC subsidy, it turns your headline claim from "assumed" to "verified," and it's a substantial hardware+firmware piece that shows real engineering depth. The **non-pet recognition gate** is the best low-effort follow-up because it patches your one obvious weakness.

Everything else is polish. Want me to spec out the load-cell integration (HX711 driver + the closed-loop feed logic + how it changes the servo control), or start with the recognition gate since it's lighter?

Does the system running on the emulator has to be the same like on actual board?

No — and for VelaPaw specifically, it **can't** be, which is fine and expected. Let me explain why, because I don't want you spending effort trying to force them to match.

**Why they fundamentally differ:** VelaPaw is a *hardware* product. It depends on real peripherals the emulator (QEMU) simply doesn't have:

| On the real board | On the emulator |
|---|---|
| OV5640 camera via LCD_CAM | no camera → mock serving embedded pet photos |
| ST7796 display over hardware SPI | goldfish virtual framebuffer |
| PCF85063 RTC over I²C | no RTC |
| servo over LEDC/PWM | nothing to drive |

So an emulator build is necessarily a **mocked, degraded** version. That's exactly why your project has two build paths — the `Makefile` (real hardware, real drivers) and the `CMakeLists.txt` (CMake/emulator, mocks). Yes — **that's exactly the right part.** It's a female DC barrel jack (the round socket) with two screw terminals (the green block, marked **−** and **+**). It accepts your 5 V adapter's barrel plug on one end and lets you wire the servo on the other. Perfect match.

## How to wire it

1. **Plug the 5 V adapter's barrel into the round socket** (the 5.5 mm barrel fits this jack directly).
2. **Screw terminal `+`** ← servo **RED** wire (V+)
3. **Screw terminal `−`** ← servo **BROWN** wire (GND) **AND** a jumper wire to the **board's GND**

That third point is the key one — the **`−` terminal is your common ground**. Both the servo's brown wire and a wire going to the ESP32-S3's GND go into that same `−` terminal (twist the two wire ends together before clamping, or use the breadboard from your kit to fan the ground out). Without that shared ground, the servo signal has no reference and won't work.

4. **Servo ORANGE** wire → board **GPIO43** (the signal — this does *not* touch the power adapter).

So the full picture:

```
5V adapter ──barrel──►  [ female jack ]
                          +  ── servo RED (V+)
                          −  ── servo BROWN (GND)  ┬─ board GND  (common ground)
                                                    
servo ORANGE ─────────────────────────────────────► board GPIO43 (signal)
```

## One thing to double-check
Make sure the adapter is **center-positive** (almost all are — the center pin = `+`). If your servo ever behaves oddly or gets warm doing nothing, swap `+`/`−`, but standard adapters are center-positive so it should be right.

That connector + a 5 V/≥2 A adapter = your servo power sorted. With the servo, screws, jumpers/breadboard, and this, your electronics BOM is complete — just confirm the adapter is **5 V and ≥2 A** when you order it.

1	# VelaPaw — feeder hardware
2	
3	Gravity hopper → **paddle rotor** → chute → bowl, driven by one hobby servo on GPIO43.
4	
5	## Why a rotor and not a flap
6	
7	A flap's dose depends on how long it stays open **and** how full the hopper is — the same 800 ms drops noticeably more food when the hopper is heavy. A rotor pocket holds a fixed volume, so the dose depends only on how many pockets you index. Since the product claim is *per-pet portion control*, a mechanism that drifts as the hopper empties would quietly undermine it.
8	
9	The MG90S is a 180° servo, so the rotor can't spin continuously. Each pocket is **one oscillation**: sweep forward 60° (a full pocket travels to the outlet and drops), then sweep back (the empty pocket returns under the inlet and refills).
10	
11	```
12	grams = pockets × GRAMS_PER_POCKET
13	```
14	
15	## Bill of materials
16	
17	| Item | Notes |
18	|---|---|
19	| **MG90S servo** ×2 | **Metal gear.** The plastic-gear SG90 is the same size and price and will strip its teeth the first time kibble jams the rotor. Buy a spare. Must be the standard **180°** version, not continuous-rotation. |
20	| **5 V supply, ≥2 A** | For the servo **only**. |
21	| **470–1000 µF electrolytic**, 16 V | Across the servo's 5 V and GND, physically close to the servo. |
22	| Female–female jumpers, small breadboard or screw terminal | To join the grounds. |
23	| PLA or PETG filament | PLA is fine for dry kibble; PETG if you want to wash the parts. |
24	
25	No motor driver, level shifter or PWM chip is needed — the ESP32-S3's LEDC peripheral generates the 50 Hz signal in hardware and drives the servo's signal pin directly at 3.3 V.
26	
27	## Wiring
28	
29	```
30	  USB ──> ESP32-S3 (3.3 V logic)
31	                │
32	                └── GPIO43 ──────────────> servo SIGNAL (orange)
33	
34	  5 V PSU ──┬──────────────────────────── servo V+ (red)
35	            └── 1000 µF ──┐
36	                          │
37	  PSU GND ──┬─────────────┴─────────────── servo GND (brown)
38	            │
39	  board GND ┘        ← COMMON GROUND, mandatory
40	```
41	
42	**Never power the servo from the board's 3.3 V or 5 V pin.** A stalling MG90S pulls close to an amp in spikes; the ESP32-S3 browns out and resets mid-feed. The two supplies share **ground only** — never tie their 5 V rails together.
43	
44	**GPIO43 is also UART0 TX.** The console runs over USB-CDC so the pin should be free, but if the servo twitches at boot, that's console traffic leaking onto the signal line — move `SERVO_PIN` to 40/41/42/47/48 in the board file.
45	
46	## Printing
47	
48	All parts print without supports. PLA/PETG, 0.2 mm layers, 3 perimeters.
49	
50	```bash
51	openscad -D 'part="rotor"'       -o rotor.stl       velapaw_feeder.scad
52	openscad -D 'part="housing"'     -o housing.stl     velapaw_feeder.scad
53	openscad -D 'part="plate_servo"' -o plate_servo.stl velapaw_feeder.scad
54	openscad -D 'part="plate_idle"'  -o plate_idle.stl  velapaw_feeder.scad
55	openscad -D 'part="hopper"'      -o hopper.stl      velapaw_feeder.scad
56	```
57	
58	Open the file with no `-D` to preview the assembly.
59	
60	**Before printing `plate_servo`, measure your own servo with calipers** and check `SERVO_BODY_L`, `SERVO_TAB_SPAN`, `SERVO_SCREW_SPAN` and `SERVO_SHAFT_DX` at the top of the `.scad`. MG90S clones vary by a millimetre or two, and the servo plate is the only part where that matters.
61	
62	## Assembly
63	
64	1. Screw the servo into `plate_servo` from behind; its flange sits flush in the recess.
65	2. Screw the round horn into the recess in the rotor hub (2 × M2).
66	3. Drop the rotor into the `housing` bore and press it onto the servo spline.
67	4. Fit `plate_idle` on the far end — its boss is the rotor's stub axle.
68	5. Bolt both plates to the housing (4 × M3).
69	6. Plug the `hopper` spigot into the inlet; put a bowl under the outlet.
70	
71	## Calibration — do this once
72	
73	1. Fill the hopper.
74	2. Dispense a single pocket.
75	3. Weigh what lands in the bowl.
76	4. Put that number in `GRAMS_PER_POCKET` in `board/esp32s3_st7789.c` and rebuild.
77	
78	Portions are then correct at any hopper level, for the life of the machine. If you want a different dose granularity, change `WIDTH` in the `.scad` (pocket volume scales linearly with it) and re-calibrate.
79	
80	`POCKETS` in the `.scad` must always equal `ROTOR_POCKETS` in the board file.
81

2. The **bowl** positioned under the outlet

- **Simplest, no design needed:** the base can just be a **flat board/plate** (wood or printed) — bolt a bracket that holds the feeder upright, set the bowl under the outlet, and screw a post beside it for the cradle. Fabricate to fit your bench.
- **I design a printable base/frame** — a proper chassis with a feeder cradle, a bowl recess, and the camera post as one integrated part. That needs a couple of decisions from you: **bowl diameter/height**, and **how tall** you want the feeder to stand (approach clearance for the pet).

This is a nicely engineered file — the comments, print-orientation planning, and the "caliper before printing" flags are all good practice. But there's one issue that's more than an improvement: the indexing scheme as described in the header doesn't work, and it's fixable in firmware before you print anything.
1. The 60° oscillation can't dispense (critical)
Your inlet and outlet are 180° apart (one slot straight through, top and bottom). The header says: sweep forward 60°, a full pocket travels to the outlet, sweep back, the empty pocket refills. But a pocket filled at the top needs to travel 180° to reach the outlet — and an oscillation has zero net rotation, so pockets can never ratchet around the wheel. Each pocket only ever visits its home position and home+60°. Trace it:

Only pockets whose 60° arc includes the top ever fill.
Only pockets whose arc includes the bottom ever dump.
No pocket's ±60° arc includes both, because they're 180° apart.

Result: the initial charge dispenses once during the first few strokes, then the machine dead-heads forever. Full pockets park at positions that never reach the outlet.
Firmware-only fix: use full 180° sweeps with a dwell at each end. Then it works, and I traced the steady state: the pocket starting at the top carries its fill down to the outlet on the forward stroke; the pocket that started at the bottom ends up at the top, fills during the dwell, and dumps on the return stroke. So one full oscillation = 2 pockets ≈ 8–9 g, consistent cycle-to-cycle, so your weigh-once calibration still holds — just calibrate GRAMS_PER_CYCLE instead of per-pocket. Granularity of ~9 g is fine for pet meals. (Two side pockets end up as permanent dead storage riding the wheel — harmless, but kibble in them goes stale; worth a note.)
Hardware fix, if you want true 1-pocket granularity: swap the MG90S for a 28BYJ-48 stepper + ULN2003 (~$2). Continuous rotation, precise 60° indexing, and the "grams = pockets × GRAMS_PER_POCKET" story in your contest writeup becomes literally true. Given portion control is VelaPaw's core claim, I'd lean this way — but the 180°-sweep servo version is a legitimate fallback.
2. Jamming at the inlet shear edge
Classic rotary-valve failure: a kibble caught between the advancing vane tip and the inlet window edge gets pinched. At the vane tip (r = 28.4 mm), the MG90S's 2.2 kg·cm stall torque gives only ~0.77 kgf of force — one hard kibble can stall it, and a stalled MG90S has no feedback to tell the firmware. Mitigations:

Chamfer/bevel the downstream inlet edge (inside the housing) so kibble gets deflected back up rather than sheared.
Firmware retry: if a dose is commanded, back off 15–20° and re-sweep — blind, but effective since you can't sense stall.
The stepper option helps here too: you can detect missed steps indirectly, and the 28BYJ-48 geared down has more usable torque.

3. Asymmetric clearance on the servo pocket
In plate_servo(), the pocket is cube([SERVO_BODY_L + CLEAR, ...]) after translating by -SERVO_BODY_L/2 — so all the clearance lands on one side, shifting the pocket (and thus the shaft) by CLEAR/2 = 0.2 mm. You marked SERVO_SHAFT_DX as critical, so fix the centering:
scadtranslate([-(SERVO_BODY_L + CLEAR)/2, -(SERVO_BODY_W + CLEAR)/2, -0.1])
    cube([SERVO_BODY_L + CLEAR, SERVO_BODY_W + CLEAR, 4.2]);
Same pattern in the flange recess and, less critically, the hopper throat.
4. Nothing holds the hopper on
It saddles onto the drum but has no registration or fastener — it'll get knocked off by a determined cat (your target user). Cheapest fix: extend two of the housing screw posts upward into bosses and give the hopper neck matching ears, or add a pair of locating pins on the drum crown that drop into sockets in the saddle.
Minor points

The pocket-volume comment uses BORE_R but the pocket is bounded by ROTOR_R, and ignores vane displacement. Real volume ≈ π(28.4² − 8²)/6 × 38 − vane ≈ 12.4 cm³ → ~4.3 g/pocket, not 5. Calibration makes this moot, but the contest doc shouldn't overstate it.
$fn = 96 globally makes previews sluggish; use $fn = $preview ? 40 : 96;.
The 34 mm bridge over the inlet/outlet windows will print, but a 45° chamfer on the window tops makes it bulletproof and costs nothing.
The stub-axle fit (6 mm boss in a 6.8 mm socket) is sloppy — fine at this speed, but tightening to +0.3 mm total would reduce rotor wobble and keep the running clearance honest.

The one thing I'd do before anything else is fix the header comment and the matching firmware constant — right now esp32s3_st7789.c presumably implements the 60° oscillation, which would demo as "dispenses once, then nothing," the worst possible contest failure mode.

A ±60° wobble only ever visits home and home+60°; the ~108° of solid wall between the inlet and outlet zones can't be crossed.  * hopper. One pocket holds a FIXED VOLUME of kibble, so the portion depends on
 * how much the rotor turns -- NOT on how long a gate stays open, and NOT on how
 * full the hopper is. That is the entire reason for the rotor: a flap's dose
 * grows with hopper weight, which would quietly wreck the per-pet portion
 * control the product is built on.
 *
 * ---- WHY A FULL 180-DEGREE SWEEP, NOT A SMALL WOBBLE --------------------------
 * The inlet (top) and outlet (bottom) are 180 degrees apart, and the MG90S can
 * only oscillate (no continuous spin). A SHORT sweep + return has ZERO net
 * rotation, so a pocket filled at the inlet can never travel the 180 deg to the
 * outlet -- the machine would drop its initial charge a few times and then
 * DEAD-HEAD forever. (This was the original 60-deg bug.)
 *
 * The fix is a FULL 180-degree oscillation with a dwell at each end:
 *   HOME(0) --sweep--> 180 : the pocket under the inlet rides down to the outlet
 *                            and drops; the pocket that was at the outlet is now
 *                            under the inlet.
 *   dwell                  : that pocket fills from the hopper.
 *   180 --sweep--> HOME(0) : the just-filled pocket rides back to the outlet and
 *                            drops.

 *  parked there can go stale. Harmless, but empty the hopper for long idle.)
 *
 * 1000us = 0 deg, 2000us = 180 deg.

#define SERVO_HOME_US        1000           /* rotor at 0 deg (rest)   */
#define SERVO_FULL_US        2000           /* rotor at 180 deg        */
#define SERVO_MOVE_MS        450            /* time for one 180 sweep  */
#define SERVO_DWELL_MS       350            /* fill/drop settle per end */

455	 * pocket has time to FILL under the inlet and DROP at the outlet (see the block

458	{
459	  servo_set_us(SERVO_FULL_US);                 /* carry inlet pocket -> outlet */
460	  nxsig_usleep(SERVO_MOVE_MS * 1000);
461	  nxsig_usleep(SERVO_DWELL_MS * 1000);         /* new pocket fills at the inlet */
462	  servo_set_us(SERVO_HOME_US);                 /* carry it back -> outlet       */

464	  nxsig_usleep(SERVO_DWELL_MS * 1000);         /* drop settles                  */

470	int board_feeder_dispense(int grams)

473	  int i;
474	
475	  if (grams <= 0) return -1;
476	
477	  /* round to the nearest whole cycle; always give at least one */
478	  cycles = (grams + GRAMS_PER_CYCLE / 2) / GRAMS_PER_CYCLE;
479	  if (cycles < 1) cycles = 1;

input.old_string:
The MG90S is a 180° servo, so the rotor can't spin continuously. Each pocket is **one oscillation**: sweep forward 60° (a full pocket travels to the outlet and drops), then sweep back (the empty pocket returns under the inlet and refills).

```
grams = pockets × GRAMS_PER_POCKET
```

## Bill of materials

| Item | Notes |
|---|---|
| **MG90S servo** ×2 | **Metal gear.** The plastic-gear SG90 is the same size and price and will strip its teeth the first time kibble jams the rotor. Buy a spare. Must be the standard **180°** version, not continuous-rotation. |
| **5 V supply, ≥2 A** | For the servo **only**. |
| **470–1000 µF electrolytic**, 16 V | Across the servo's 5 V and GND, physically close to the servo. |
| Female–female jumpers, small breadboard or screw terminal | To join the grounds. |
| PLA or PETG filament | PLA is fine for dry kibble; PETG if you want to wash the parts. |

No motor driver, level shifter or PWM chip is needed — the ESP32-S3's LEDC peripheral generates the 50 Hz signal in hardware and drives the servo's signal pin directly at 3.3 V.

## Wiring

```
  USB ──> ESP32-S3 (3.3 V logic)
                │
                └── GPIO43 ──────────────> servo SIGNAL (orange)

  5 V PSU ──┬──────────────────────────── servo V+ (red)
            └── 1000 µF ──┐
                          │
  PSU GND ──┬─────────────┴─────────────── servo GND (brown)
            │
  board GND ┘        ← COMMON GROUND, mandatory
```

**Never power the servo from the board's 3.3 V or 5 V pin.** A stalling MG90S pulls close to an amp in spikes; the ESP32-S3 browns out and resets mid-feed. The two supplies share **ground only** — never tie their 5 V rails together.

**GPIO43 is also UART0 TX.** The console runs over USB-CDC so the pin should be free, but if the servo twitches at boot, that's console traffic leaking onto the signal line — move `SERVO_PIN` to 40/41/42/47/48 in the board file.
input.new_string:
The rotor is driven by a **28BYJ-48 stepper** (via a ULN2003 board), which rotates **continuously in one direction** — so pockets ratchet inlet→outlet and per-pocket dosing is exact:

```
grams = pockets × GRAMS_PER_POCKET
```

> **Why a stepper, not a servo.** An MG90S servo can only *oscillate*, and with the inlet and outlet 180° apart a zero-net-rotation wobble can never carry a pocket across — it dispenses the initial charge then dead-heads. The stepper's continuous spin is what makes the rotary valve actually work, and it makes the portion-control claim literally true. (The geared 28BYJ-48 also has strong low-speed torque, which resists kibble jams.)

## Bill of materials

| Item | Notes |
|---|---|
| **28BYJ-48 stepper + ULN2003 driver** (5 V bundle) | The **5 V** version — runs off the same 5 V supply below. Get the motor+driver bundle. |
| **5 V supply, ≥2 A** | Powers the ULN2003/motor. Common **ground** with the ESP32; never tie the 5 V rails together. |
| Female–female jumpers | 4 signal lines (IN1–IN4) + 5 V + GND to the ULN2003. |
| PLA / PETG (or JLC nylon) | PLA is fine for dry kibble; PETG/nylon if you want to wash the parts. |

The **ULN2003 board is the driver** — no separate PWM chip; the ESP32-S3 just toggles 4 GPIOs through the half-step sequence. (No servo → the 470 µF servo-inrush cap is no longer needed.)

## Wiring

```
  ESP32-S3 (3.3 V logic)            ULN2003 driver board          28BYJ-48
    GPIO12 ─────────────────────────> IN1
    GPIO13 ─────────────────────────> IN2                         (5-pin
    GPIO15 ─────────────────────────> IN3            motor  ────►  connector)
    GPIO16 ─────────────────────────> IN4
                                      +   ◄── 5 V PSU +
                                      −   ◄──┬─ 5 V PSU −
  board GND ───────────────────────────────┘   ← COMMON GROUND, mandatory
```

- **GPIO12/13/15/16** are the ES8311 audio-codec lines; VelaPaw uses no audio, so they're free (all ESP32→codec directions, safe to drive). Change them in the board file (`STEP_IN1..4`) if you ever add audio.
- **Power the ULN2003 from the separate 5 V supply, not the board**, and share **ground only**. The 28BYJ-48 draws ~240 mA/phase — fine for a 2 A supply.
- The ULN2003's on-board LEDs show the coil sequence — handy for confirming it's stepping.

Great question, and that render is a strong vision to aim at. Let me be honest about what's realistic and give you a clear recommendation, because there's an important reality gap here.

## What that image actually is
That's a **professional industrial-design render of an injection-molded product** — smooth ABS shell, compound curves, everything hidden inside a sculpted body, 380 mm tall. It's what VelaPaw would look like *after* tooling and a factory. It's beautiful, and notably it already shows your feature set: touch display, camera, portion control, **load-cell weight monitoring** (the upgrade we discussed), a dispense motor (your stepper). So it's a great *target*.

## The honest gap
Two hard limits stand between that render and what you can build now:
1. **Injection molding vs. 3D printing.** That smooth monolithic shell is designed for a mold. Printed (FDM/resin), a body like that comes out with visible layer lines, needs supports, must be **split into sections** (380 mm > any print bed), and needs sanding + priming + painting to look like the render. That's a lot of finishing work.
2. **OpenSCAD is the wrong tool for that aesthetic.** OpenSCAD is CSG — excellent for mechanical parts (which is why our feeder/cradle came out clean), but poor at the sculpted compound curves that render lives on. Matching that look would fight the tool the whole way and still come out faceted.

## My recommendation — and it's a strategic one
**Don't try to replicate the render in plastic. Use it as your product vision, and keep the physical build functional-but-clean.** Here's the split I'd do:

- **Physical prototype (what you print & demo):** a *simplified* enclosing shell — a clean vertical column that **hides the mechanism**, screen/camera on top, kibble container in the body, bowl at the base. Mostly flat/gently-faceted surfaces that OpenSCAD can do and that print without drama. It won't match the render's polish, but it'll look like a *product* instead of an exposed A-frame. Achievable in your timeline.
- **Submission / pitch:** put a polished render like that one in your README and defense as the **"industrial-design vision / production target,"** clearly labeled, *next to* the working prototype. This is exactly what hardware startups do — show the working engineering **and** the vision render. It's honest and it's compelling.

**Why this way:** the contest scores your **working on-device AI and engineering** (Technical Difficulty 30, Completeness 20) — not shell finish. A device that *works* (recognizes the pet, dispenses the right portion) plus a vision render tells a far stronger, more honest story than two months poured into a shell that print quality would undercut anyway. You've got a genuinely impressive *working* machine; don't trade that for cosmetics.

## Concrete options
1. **Design the simplified column shell** — I repackage the mechanism vertically (drum lower in the body, container above, chute to the bowl, screen on top) into a printable 2–3 piece enclosure. Real work, but doable, and gives you the product silhouette.
2. **Keep the functional stand** (what we have) and **make the render your vision asset** — fastest path, focus the rest of your time on assembling + calibrating + the demo video.
3. **Both** — simplified shell for the demo *and* the render for the pitch.

My honest lean: **option 2 now**, and if you finish assembly/calibration with time to spare before Sept 20, do the simplified shell (option 1). The working device + vision render is the submission that wins.

text:
Yes, it's doable — and for a Chinese contest a bilingual UI is a genuine plus. But let me be straight about what it actually takes, because there are two separate pieces and one of them is the real work.

## Where the UI stands today

- The UI ([ui_lvgl.c](contest2026_043_CircuitForge/app/velapaw/ui/ui_lvgl.c)) is a 4-tab LVGL app with **~79 hardcoded English strings** written inline (`lv_label_set_text(l, "No pets yet - enroll one")`).
- The font is **Montserrat** (`lv_font_montserrat_*`) — **Latin/ASCII only. It has zero Chinese glyphs.** If you set a label to 中文 today, you'd get empty boxes.
- There's no settings screen and no string-lookup layer yet.

## What a language toggle needs — three parts

**1. A string table (i18n layer)** — mechanical, low-risk.
Extract the 79 strings into one table with an EN column and a ZH column, and replace each literal with a lookup keyed on a global `g_lang`:
```c
enum { STR_NO_PETS, STR_PORTION, ... };
static const char *TBL[][2] = {
  [STR_NO_PETS] = {"No pets yet - enroll one", "还没有宠物 - 请先录入"},
  ...
};
#define T(id) (TBL[id][g_lang])
```
The `_fmt` calls (`"Portion: %d g"`) stay format strings — the ZH version just carries the number in its own word order.

**2. A CJK font — this is the real cost.**
Montserrat can't render Chinese, so you must generate an LVGL font from a CJK TTF (Noto Sans CJK / Source Han Sans) containing **only the glyphs you actually use** (a few hundred chars). Via `lv_font_conv` or the online converter → a `.c` font blob compiled in. Budget roughly **50–150 KB of flash** depending on glyph count. Then labels use that font instead of Montserrat. (You have 16 MB flash, so space is fine.)

**3. The toggle + persistence** — small.
A switch or EN/中 segmented control (in the header or a small Settings area), saving the choice to NVS/SD so it survives reboot — same pattern the feed history already uses.

## My honest recommendation

Feasibility is not in question — the font-subset step is the only non-trivial part, and it's well-trodden LVGL territory. The catch is **timing**: this touches every label in the UI and needs a real device to verify the glyphs render, and right now the repo still isn't pushed and the hardware isn't assembled. Both of those score more directly.

So I'd suggest one of two paths:

# VelaPaw UI — bilingual (English / 中文)

The UI runs in English or Chinese and switches live from the **中 / EN** toggle in
the top-right of the header (next to the bell). The choice is saved to flash and
restored on the next boot.

## How it is wired

| Piece | File | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| String table | [ui_i18n.c](ui_i18n.c) | one row per `S_*` id, `{ English, 中文 }` |
| Lookup | `T(id)` → `velapaw_tr()` | returns the current-language string |
| Switch + persist | `velapaw_lang_set()` | flips language, writes one flash cell |
| Font seam | `velapaw_font(level)` | the **only** place fonts are chosen |
| Live rebuild | `ui_build()` in [ui_lvgl.c](ui_lvgl.c) | tears down + recreates the tree so one-shot labels re-read the language |

Every label goes through `T(...)` for its text and `velapaw_font(...)` for its
font, so adding a language or a font is a change in one place, not 79.

## The one thing left: a Chinese-capable font

The stock `lv_font_montserrat_*` fonts are **Latin-only** — they have no CJK
glyphs, so with `CONFIG_VELAPAW_FONT_CJK=n` (the default) the toggle still works
but Chinese text renders as blank boxes. English is fully functional today.

To make Chinese actually render:

1. **Generate a subset font** from a CJK TTF (Noto Sans CJK SC / Source Han Sans),
   containing only ASCII + the glyphs this UI uses. Using LVGL's
   [font converter](https://github.com/lvgl/lv_font_conv):

   ```bash
   # collect every Chinese glyph the UI can show (from the 中文 column)
   #   -> feed the unique code points to --range or --symbols
   lv_font_conv --font NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf \
       --size 14 --bpp 2 --format lvgl \
       --symbols "$(cat ui_i18n.c | grep -o '[一-龥]' | sort -u | tr -d '\n')" \
       --range 0x20-0x7F \
       -o velapaw_font_cjk_14.c
   # repeat at --size 16 and --size 20 -> _16.c and _20.c
   ```

   The three blobs must define `velapaw_font_cjk_14 / _16 / _20`
   (rename the `lv_font_t` in each generated file to match, or pass
   `--force-fast-kern-format` / edit the symbol name).

2. **Add the three `.c` files** to `CSRCS` (Makefile) and the CMake `VELAPAW_SRCS`
   list, right next to `ui/ui_i18n.c`.

3. **Enable the option:** `CONFIG_VELAPAW_FONT_CJK=y`. `velapaw_font()` then returns
   the CJK font for every level, and — because that font also carries Latin —
   both languages render from it.

Budget ~50–150 KB of flash for the glyph subset (a few hundred characters × 3
sizes). The board has 16 MB, so this is comfortable.

## Adding / editing strings

1. Add an `S_*` id to the enum in [ui_i18n.h](ui_i18n.h).
2. Add its `{ "English", "中文" }` row to `g_strtab[]` in [ui_i18n.c](ui_i18n.c).
3. Use `T(S_YOUR_ID)` at the call site (with `lv_label_set_text` or
   `lv_label_set_text_fmt`).

Rows that carry `printf` conversions (`%d`, `%s`, `%.2f`, …) **must keep the same
conversions in both languages** — the same values are formatted into whichever
string is active.

## What I built

**Wired into the UI** — [ui_lvgl.c](contest2026_043_CircuitForge/app/velapaw/ui/ui_lvgl.c):

**Build + docs**: registered in both Makefile and CMake, added `CONFIG_VELAPAW_FONT_CJK`, and wrote [README_I18N.md](contest2026_043_CircuitForge/app/velapaw/ui/README_I18N.md).

- Braces/parens balanced; no dangling locals from the refactor; no leftover English literals.

With the font option **off (default), English is fully working, but Chinese renders as blank boxes** — Montserrat has no CJK glyphs. Making 中文 actually display needs a generated subset font (`velapaw_font_cjk_14/16/20`) linked in + `CONFIG_VELAPAW_FONT_CJK=y`; the exact `lv_font_conv` command is in README_I18N.md. ### 1. Pull the changed files into the VM tree

### 2. Build

Exact command used (Noto Sans SC Regular OTF, one per size):

```bash
lv_font_conv --font NotoSansSC-Regular.otf --size 14 --bpp 4 --format lvgl \
    --range 0x20-0x7F,<the 150 CJK code points> --no-compress \
    -o velapaw_font_cjk_14.c        # repeat --size 16 / 20
```

The glyph set is derived straight from the 中文 column of `ui_i18n.c`, so if you
add Chinese strings, regenerate (widen `--range`).

> **License note:** Noto Sans SC is OFL 1.1 — fine to embed and publish. Keep the
> OFL attribution with the repo. Do **not** substitute a Microsoft font
> (YaHei/SimSun) in the shipped build; their EULAs don't cover redistribution.

### Historical: why this was needed

The stock `lv_font_montserrat_*` fonts are **Latin-only** — with
`CONFIG_VELAPAW_FONT_CJK=n` (the default) the toggle still works but Chinese text
renders as blank boxes. English is fully functional either way.

# Contest Log Collector — openvela AI 大赛 AI Coding 日志归集

为 openvela AI 大赛提供 AI Coding 日志归集能力,**工作区感应、对话结束自动入仓**。

## 核心架构

```
       ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │ 门控: 当前目录向上能找到 .repo/ ?                    │
       │   否 → 不在 openvela 工作区 → 完全不采集             │
       │   是 → 在 openvela 工作区 → 进入采集                 │
       └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                               │ (在工作区内)
                               ↓
       ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │ 对话结束自动写入: demo 仓 logs/<login>/              │
       │ 只写文件,不自动 commit/push                         │
       │ 选手 git push 时跟代码一起上 GitHub                  │
       └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**关键安全特性**: 用"是否在 openvela 工作区(`.repo/`)内"作为隐私门控 —— 选手在个人项目(工作区外)跟 AI 聊的对话**完全不采集**;只有在比赛工作区内的对话才会自动写入选手仓 `logs/`,且工具自身**永远不会 git push**,上传由选手控制。

## 自动入仓(默认,无需操作)

在 openvela 工作区内跟 AI 工具(Claude Code / OpenCode / Codex)对话,会话结束时日志会**自动写入**选手仓的 `logs/<github_login>/`。选手只需在提交代码时一起 push:

```bash
git add logs/
git commit -s -m "logs: capture session"
git push
```

## (可选)手动补导

正常流程不需要,但你可以用手动工具查看清单或补导某次会话。

> ⚠️ 手动工具的 `--confirm`:不加时只预览不写文件。手动补导仅用于补救/管理,正常对话已自动入仓。

  - `~/.claude/contest-collector.env` — 选手身份(TEAM_ID + GITHUB_LOGIN)
  - `~/.claude/contest-shared/` — snapshot core + 全局 hook 脚本
  - `~/.claude/settings.json` — 注册 Stop / SessionEnd hook(deep merge,保留原有配置)
  - `~/.claude/contest-collector-staging/` — staging 区
- **选手仓**:
  - `.claude/shared/` — snapshot core(给 export 工具用)
  - `.claude/commands/contest-snapshot.md` — slash command
  - `.opencode/plugins/contest-collector.js` — OpenCode plugin
  - `../.claude/skills/contest-log-collector/tools/export-session.py` + `render-log.py` + `validate-log.py`
  - `schema/event.schema.json` + `manifest.schema.json`
  - `JUDGE_GUIDE.md` — 评委指南
  - `USAGE.md` — 选手手册
  - `.gitignore` — 已加日志相关排除

## 数据契约

JSONL 每条事件必含字段:

- `schema_version` — 当前 1.0
- `session_id` — AI 工具内部 session ID
- `team_id` — 对应仓库的官方匿名编号
- `github_login` — 当前组员 GitHub username
- `tool` — opencode / claude-code / codex / kiro
- `seq` — session 内单调递增(防作弊核心)
- `ts` — ISO 8601 UTC 时间戳
- `role` — user / assistant / tool / system

## 安全特性

- **工作区门控**: 只在 openvela 工作区(向上能找到 `.repo/`)内采集,工作区外的对话(含个人项目)完全不采集
- **不自动上传**: 自动入仓只写本机仓内 `logs/` 文件,工具自身从不 `git push`,上传由选手控制
- **自动脱敏**: 默认正则覆盖 `sk-*` (API key) / `ghp_*` (GitHub token) / `Bearer *` (auth header)
- **TEAM_ID 缺失主动拒绝**: 防止数据归属错乱
- **多人组天然安全**: 按 `<github_login>/` 一人一目录,组员之间互不干扰

What do you think of this

Design‑wise it's genuinely strong — it reads like a real product analytics screen: the intake bars with a baseline overlay, a dedicated appetite line, and a BCS gauge with a trend spark. That's a clear, professional direction and I like it as a north star.

But I want to be straight about the **reality gap**, because this mockup is a portrait, high‑DPI render and the device is the opposite of that:

**The constraints it has to survive:**
- **480×320 landscape**, not tall portrait — you can't stack three big cards; the tab would scroll (it already does), and each card has to be squat/wide.
- **Bit‑bang panel at ~3 fps.** Every chart and especially the **filled gauge arc** is a lot of pixels to repaint. Static is fine (redraw only on data change); anything animated would crawl.
- **LVGL charting limits.** Some of this isn't a straight drop‑in.

**Element by element:**
- **7‑day bars** — easy, and the green/blue coloring is trivial styling (we already have the bars). ✅
- **Dotted baseline over the bars** — *not* a freebie: LVGL 9 charts are one type per chart, so you can't just add a line series on top of bars. It needs a manual draw callback (or a second overlaid chart). Doable, moderate. ⚠️
- **Appetite line chart** (separate card, dates, the red "today" marker, the `2` tooltip) — a second `lv_chart` in line mode + a cursor line + a manual label. Doable, moderate. The 6 date labels are tight at 480 px wide. ⚠️

And what you saw on **Next Day (demo)** is actually *correct*, not a bug. The colors are relative to the **window's average**, so when you advance a day the whole history shifts (yesterday's numbers slide over, today resets), the average recomputes, and every bar re‑evaluates above/below that new average — so the split legitimately changes. The chart is just faithfully re‑reading the new data.

That said — I think the *relative* threshold is the wrong choice here, and it's exactly why it feels jumpy. Two downsides:
- It always forces ~half green / half blue (it's relative to itself), and
- A given day flips color just because the window moved, even though that day's actual intake didn't change.

**Better: color against the pet's baseline** (their normal daily intake). Then green = "ate at or above normal that day," blue = "under‑ate" — which is the actual health signal, it's **stable** (a day keeps its meaning when you advance), and it won't wholesale‑flip on Next Day. It's a one‑line change (compare each bar to `store_baseline_g` instead of the window mean).

---
name: velapaw-trends-dashboard
description: "VelaPaw Trends tab rework on hardware — colored intake bars + appetite line chart + BCS gauge (LVGL 9.1); the API gotchas that took iteration"
metadata:
  type: project
---

VelaPaw **Trends tab** reworked to match a shared product mockup, running on the ESP32-S3 (2026-07-21). Three stacked cards, all in `app/velapaw/ui/ui_lvgl.c` (build_trends/refresh_trends + helpers). Bilingual via [[velapaw-i18n]]. Confirmed good on the panel ("perfect").

## What's there
1. **Colored intake bars** — the existing `lv_chart` BAR, recolored per-bar: green if that day >= the window average, blue if below (the colour split IS the baseline, so no separate average line). Avg is computed over **completed days only** (exclude today = last index; today is often 0 g and would drag the mean so every past day reads above-average = all green).
2. **Appetite trend** — a second `lv_chart` LINE card: each day's intake as % of the pet's `daily_limit_g` (0-100), COL_ACCENT line.
3. **BCS gauge** — a 3-zone semicircular dial: three `lv_arc` bands (amber Under 180-240°, green Ideal 240-300°, red Over 300-360°; LVGL arc 0°=3 o'clock, CW, so 180-360 = top half) + an `lv_line` needle + a hub. GA_D=150, arc width 18, needle width 7 **white** for a real reading / grey for "no reading", white-ringed hub, big class label below. Needle tip offsets are hardcoded per class (only 3 classes) — no trig/math.h: under=(-54,-31), ideal=(0,-62), over=(54,-31), NA=(0,-36).

## LVGL 9.1 API gotchas (each cost a cycle — the console is dead during any wedge, so it's build+flash+eyeball only)
- **Per-bar chart colour**: use the `LV_EVENT_DRAW_TASK_ADDED` event + `lv_obj_add_flag(chart, LV_OBJ_FLAG_SEND_DRAW_TASK_EVENTS)`. In 9.1 read the base dsc via **`task->draw_dsc`** (the getter `lv_draw_task_get_draw_dsc()` is **9.2-only** → undefined reference at link). `lv_draw_task_get_fill_dsc()` DOES exist in 9.1. The point index is **`base->id1`** (NOT id2 — id2 is the series index; with a single series id2 is always 0 → every bar reads vals[0] → all one colour).
- **No `lv_meter`** in 9.x. `lv_scale` exists and `lv_scale_set_line_needle_value` IS in 9.1, but the section range/style setters are NOT (they're later) — so I built the coloured zones from stacked `lv_arc` instead of lv_scale sections.
- Forward-declare `refresh_bcs_gauge` before refresh_trends (it's defined after, but called by it).

## Data note
BCS (`velapaw_store_get_bcs`) is a 3-class score set only when a pet is **recognized** (the 2nd model majority-votes). Empty demo data → gauge shows grey "-" (no reading). To demo the needle swinging, recognize a pet on the Recognize tab first. No per-day BCS history is stored, so the mockup's little BCS sparkline was NOT built.
